summary:
I built and measured a working single-provider HE mask-preprocessing prototype on this CPU box (2 BLAS threads). It produces W r mod 2^40 bit-exactly on a real Qwen2.5-0.5B gate slice (4864x896), a 7B-shaped qkv slice (4608x3584) and a worst-case 7B down slice (64x18944, |W|=127). The design choice that matters is token-batched column packing with coefficient encoding. Ciphertext i carries mask r_i for N=4096 future tokens. W touches ciphertexts only through integer scalars, so (1) the plaintext modulus can be t=2^40 exactly (the PGW ring, nothing to bridge); (2) Q can be 2^64, a power of two, so the server's work is one plain GEMM mod 2^64 with no NTT and no rotations: the existing ringmm at K=64, 8 int8 GEMM passes against 5 for today's K40 factory; (3) the client only does one encrypt per input and one decrypt per output per 4096 tokens. The same product through OpenFHE's elementwise ct x pt API costs 20.8 ns per token-MAC, against 0.071 ns in GEMM form (about 290x).

Best variant (B): fixed public a_i with a fresh secret per batch, plus a one-time hint H = W A mod 2^64 kept by the client (45.6 GB for 7B). The server returns only b compressed to 44 bits. Variant C adds upload compression: the mask is defined as the high 40 bits of u - a s for a public PRG value u, so the client uploads a 25-bit correction instead of 64 bits. Both are verified exact.

Projected for 7B per token (from measured slices):
- Customer storage no longer grows with token volume. Instead there is a fixed rolling buffer of one batch, 4096 tokens = 28.5 GB, plus the 45.6 GB hint for B/C. Today the store grows 6.95 MB per token, about 7 TB/day at 1M tokens/day.
- The customer runs no GPU factory, only CPU crypto: 0.42 s per token measured with numpy FFT. An NTT-grade client is estimated at about 0.16 s.
- Our GPU does the factory work: about 106k tokens/h per T4 for B/C, derived from the team's 169k/h K40 factory rate times 5/8.
- The cost is network traffic. On top of today's 11.1 MB/token online traffic, B adds 6.65 MB up + 7.65 MB down = 14.3 MB/token, and C adds 2.6 + 7.65 = 10.2 MB/token. The download of about 44 bits per output element cannot go much lower: the client must receive about 40 bits of W r per output.

Privacy rests on RLWE with N=4096, Q=2^64, ternary secret, sigma=3.2. That is far inside the HE Security Standard's 128-bit bound (logQ <= 109 at N=4096). The server sees only RLWE ciphertexts. Integrity comes from Freivalds on the decrypted mask batch (u.M == (uW).R mod 2^40), which is cheap, and the client aborts and discards the batch on failure. Measured noise margins: worst max |noise|/Delta was 0.11 for A and 0.044 for B against the 0.5 limit, including the worst-case d_in=18944 down shape.

options.name: B: RLWE token-batched GEMM preprocessing with fixed public a + one-time client hint (Q=2^64, t=2^40, N=4096) - RECOMMENDED
options.how_it_works: Per batch of N=4096 future tokens the gateway draws a fresh ternary secret s and masks R (d_in x N, uniform mod 2^40). It uploads b_i = a_i*s + e_i + 2^24*r_i mod (X^N+1, 2^64), one polynomial per input feature. The a_i are fixed forever from a public seed, so only b is sent. Our server computes Y = W @ B mod 2^64, a plain GEMM equal to PGW ringmm at K=64 (8 int8 passes on GPU), and returns b' = round(Y/2^20) (44 bits). The gateway keeps the one-time hint H = W A mod 2^64. It computes v = b'*2^20 - H*s (polynomial product via NTT/FFT, O(log N) per element) and m = round(v/2^24) mod 2^40 = W r. A Freivalds check on the decrypted batch follows, then masks go into a small JIT buffer. The online protocol is unchanged.
options.extra_compute_or_bandwidth: Measured 7B-shaped qkv slice 4608x3584 (2 BLAS threads): server 0.0714 ns per token-MAC (float64 GEMM), so 0.47 s/token CPU for full 7B (6.53e9 MACs). Derived: 0.10 s/token at the measured 1 TOPS CPU int8 rate. On GPU this is 8 int8 GEMM passes against 5 for the K40 factory, so about 106k 7B tokens/h per T4 (derived from the given 169k/h) or about 438k/h (derived from the sizing.md 8B K48 0.0066 s/slot), on OUR GPU. Customer CPU, measured numpy FFT: encrypt 198 ns per input element and decrypt 181 ns per output element per token, so 0.42 s/token for 7B. An NTT-grade client is estimated at about 0.16 s/token (OpenFHE measured 27 ns/coefficient decrypt at N=4096). Extra bandwidth per 7B token: 6.65 MB up + 7.65 MB down = 14.3 MB (analytic), on top of today's 11.1 MB online. Fixed customer footprint: hint 45.6 GB (one-time, computed once and Freivalds-verified) plus a rolling buffer of one batch, 28.5 GB.
options.security_model: Single provider. Privacy: RLWE N=4096, Q=2^64, ternary s, discrete Gaussian sigma=3.2. This is far inside the 128-bit bound of the HE Security Standard (Albrecht et al., HomomorphicEncryption.org 2018: logQ<=109 at N=4096). RLWE pseudorandomness holds for any modulus including powers of two (Peikert-Regev-Stephens-Davidowitz, STOC 2017). Reusing a fixed public a with a fresh secret per batch is the multi-secret setting, the same reuse SimplePIR makes of its public matrix (Henzinger et al., USENIX Security 2023). The server sees only ciphertexts and learns nothing about r, and r is never used except as a one-time pad. Integrity: Freivalds on the decrypted batch (u.M == (uW).R mod 2^40, about (d_in+d_out) ops per token per vector). A tampering server causes an abort; this leaks at most about 1 bit per batch about a secret that is discarded. Correctness is exact (deterministic decode margin 0.044 Delta measured at d_in=18944 worst case).
options.maturity: Prototyped here (Python/numpy, bit-exact). The primitive (linearly homomorphic RLWE, hint reuse) is deployed in the PIR literature (SimplePIR/Tiptoe), not yet in an inference product.
options.effort_to_build: Medium. The server endpoint reuses ringmm with _MAX_K raised 56->64 (ring.py comments say K<=64 works with wrap). The gateway needs an NTT-based RLWE encrypt/decrypt (or OpenFHE/HEXL), hint install with a Freivalds check, batch scheduler and buffer, and a Freivalds check on decrypted masks. Estimate 2-4 engineer-weeks.

options.name: C: variant B plus upload compression (mask defined as high bits of u - a*s)
options.how_it_works: Same as B, except that u_i comes from a public PRG seed and the client sends only c_i = e_i - ((u_i - a_i s) mod± 2^24), 25 bits signed. Then b_i = u_i + c_i is a valid encryption with fresh Gaussian noise, and the mask is DEFINED as r_i = (u_i - a_i s - rem)/2^24 (40 bits). It can be regenerated from the batch secret and public seeds. The server reconstructs b from the seed and c.
options.extra_compute_or_bandwidth: Measured on qwen 0.5B gate: exact_match=true; |c| max 2^23.0, so 25 bits per input element. The derived mask mean is 0.49999 x 2^40, consistent with uniform. 7B upload drops from 6.65 to 2.60 MB/token, so total extra traffic is 10.2 MB/token (analytic). Server cost is the same as B. The client numpy encrypt is slower (786 ns per element, unoptimised extra PRG pass), giving 0.90 s/token for 7B measured-extrapolated; optimised it should be close to B.
options.security_model: Single provider, RLWE as in B. The server's view (a, u, c) is a function of an RLWE sample: c reveals only a*s+e mod 2^24. The high 40 bits (the mask) stay pseudorandom given the low bits, because the full sample (a, a*s+e mod 2^64) is pseudorandom. Integrity is the same as B. This needs a short written proof before production.
options.maturity: Prototyped here (exact). Similar in spirit to Kyber/Saber ciphertext compression; this exact mask-definition trick is a research idea.
options.effort_to_build: Small increment over B (about 2-3 days), plus a security write-up.

options.name: Rejected: plain-LWE 'hint' used ONLINE (SimplePIR-style, no masks at all)
options.how_it_works: The gateway sends x_hat = A s + e + Delta x and the server returns W x_hat. The gateway subtracts (W A) s using a fixed hint and rounds. No preprocessing is needed.

The gateway could then just run the model itself. Batching over tokens (ring version) is impossible online because decode is sequential.

open_questions: The batch buffer is N tokens (28.5 GB for 7B, 138 GB for 70B) because each ciphertext's coefficients are all multiplied by the same W_ji, so one decrypt yields one feature for all 4096 tokens. Is that acceptable, or do we need Cheetah-style polynomial packing (per-token, server pays NTTs and sparse output extraction; not prototyped)?

Bandwidth replaces storage: B adds 14.3 MB/token (C 10.2 MB) on top of 11.1 MB online, i.e. about 10-14 TB/day of traffic at 1M tokens/day instead of 7 TB/day of disk. Is the customer's link the cheaper resource?
Hint size for B/C (45.6 GB 7B, 220 GB 70B) is one-time but large. Variant A removes it at 2.1x the download. A hint stored in NTT form would speed decrypt; worth measuring.
Client CPU numbers are numpy FFT (about 180-200 ns per element-token). A C++/HEXL NTT client mod 2^64 (2-limb CRT) is estimated at 2-3x faster but was not measured.
GPU server rate is derived (int8 GEMM pass count vs the team's factory measurements), not measured. ringmm needs _MAX_K raised to 64 and a check that the wrap is exact.
Variant C security argument (mask defined as high bits of u - a s) needs a written proof. Parameter security was taken from the HE Standard table, not run through the lattice-estimator.
A malicious server can force aborts. The leakage is 1 bit per discarded fresh secret; confirm no long-lived key reuse in the hint scheme (a is fixed but s is fresh per batch).

summary:
The recommended design is PGW-LH, "hinted MLWE masking". It removes the customer's mask factory and the per-token mask store. In their place the customer keeps a one-time hint of about 28.5 GB for 7B (as much as 4,096 tokens of today's masks) and a working buffer of about 4.6 GB. Privacy rests on MLWE with a single provider, and integrity uses Freivalds over a prime field (2^-55 per check).

Why it works:
- The customer already knows W, so no circuit privacy or noise flooding is needed.
- Masks do not depend on the data, so ciphertexts can be laid out along the token axis (coefficient j = token j). The service's "plaintext W times ciphertexts" step then becomes a plain int8 digit GEMM mod q, with no NTTs, rotations or key switching on the server.
- The public LWE matrix A is fixed, so the gateway keeps a reusable hint H = W·A (the SimplePIR trick, USENIX Security 2023). It removes W's image of the pad with a cheap ring product <H_i, s>.

The Delphi-style preprocessing round then folds into the online call:
- The gateway sends v = Δx − P, where P = <a, s> + e is an MLWE pad generated on the gateway CPU.
- The service returns z = W·v mod q (q ≈ 2^56 prime).
- The gateway decodes y = round((z + <H, s>)/Δ), which equals W·x exactly.

This needs no extra round trips, and the non-colluding factory party disappears. Costs for Qwen2.5-7B:
- Gateway CPU: 0.10 core-seconds per token, scalar (derived from the measured 46 ns per row per token).
- Our GPU: 7 int8 digit GEMMs instead of 5 online (×1.4), with no factory GEMM anywhere.
- Network: 5.8 MB up and 9.7 MB down per token, against 4.16 and 6.95 today. A truncated-z mode brings download to 6.3 MB.

I verified exactness end to end at n = 3584 and 18944 with worst-case weights. Worst noise was 2^17.6 against a 2^21 budget.

Variant A (true Delphi-style JIT preprocessing that keeps today's online protocol) also works. It needs about 15.5 MB per token of extra network and a second GEMM, so it is a migration path only. Classic HE in the online path (BumbleBee/NEXUS style) is orders of magnitude too slow: about 8 min per token for LLaMA-7B according to BumbleBee (NDSS 2025). The two-provider fallback is not needed.

options.name: PGW-LH: hinted MLWE masking (Delphi preprocessing folded into the online call)
options.how_it_works: Public A (seeded, per customer or pack) is MLWE over Z_q[X]/(X^256+1), rank 10, q a prime below 2^56 with q ≡ 1 mod 512. The service computes hint H = W·A once and the gateway verifies it with Freivalds. For each group of 256 token slots and each (layer, linear), the gateway samples secret s and noise e, then computes pads P = <a, s> + e and corrections C = <H, s> with NTTs. Online, the gateway sends v = Δx − P and the service returns z = W·v mod q (7 int8 digit GEMMs). The gateway checks u·z = (uW)·v mod q and decodes y = round((z + C)/Δ) = W·x exactly (t = 2^34, Δ ≈ 2^22).
options.extra_compute_or_bandwidth:
Customer, one time: 28.5 GB hint plus 0.39 GB A (7B); 6.2 GB for 0.5B; 138 GB for 70B. Working buffer: 4.6 GB per group of 256 tokens (7B).
Customer CPU: 0.10 core-s per 7B token, scalar C, derived from measured 46 ns per row per token over 2.22M rows. That is 1.2 cores for 1M tokens/day; 0.02 s per token for 0.5B and 0.51 s for 70B. Replaces 5.9 T4-hours per 1M tokens of factory work.
Our GPU: 7 instead of 5 int8 digit GEMMs, so about 1.4× the online GEMM. Estimated +44 to +132 H100-s per 1M tokens at 10–30% INT8 utilisation, or about +800 s if scaled from PGW's own 2 ms/token estimate; $0.04–0.7 per 1M tokens. No factory GEMM.
Network per 7B token: 5.82 MB up (was 4.16) and 9.73 MB down with full 56-bit z (was 6.95), or 6.26 MB down with truncated z.
Hint streaming: 111 MB per token from RAM at N'=256, or 28 MB per token at N'=1024.
options.security_model:
Single provider. Privacy reduces to decision-MLWE: dimension 2560, q ≈ 2^56, CBD secret, σ ≈ 3.2 error, with many secrets under one public A. That is standard and post-quantum. The 128-bit level is estimated from the HE Standard table and must be confirmed with lattice-estimator.
No circuit privacy or noise flooding is needed because W is public to the customer. There is no factory or partner party and no non-collusion assumption.
Integrity: Freivalds over F_q at 2^-55 per check, so c = 1 suffices. Abort events depend only on u and the service's deviation, not on s, e or x, so selective failure leaks nothing about data. A malformed hint is caught at setup by Freivalds against uW and A, before any secret is used.
Leaks: nothing beyond timing and size. The pad slot single-use rule still applies (reuse leaks Δ(x1−x2)). Truncated-z mode weakens this to at most 1 bit leaked about the noise at an abort.
options.maturity: research idea / prototyped here. It combines published pieces: SimplePIR hint (USENIX Sec 2023), Cheetah coefficient encoding (USENIX Sec 2022), Delphi preprocessing (USENIX Sec 2020), and the MLWE used in Kyber/FrodoKEM. I know of no deployment for LLM linear layers.

options.name: Variant A: JIT HE preprocessing, Delphi-shaped, online protocol unchanged
options.how_it_works: The gateway uploads an MLWE encryption of today's mask r along the token axis, b = <a,s> + e + Δr, using the same fixed A and hint H. The service returns W·b mod q. The gateway decodes W r mod 2^K = round((W·b − <H,s>)/Δ) and keeps it only in a small JIT buffer; the online K40 protocol is unchanged. In Delphi's 'service keeps s' form, the service holds a share S and returns W·x̂ − S, which moves the buffer to our side.
options.extra_compute_or_bandwidth:
Extra network per 7B token: +5.8 MB up and +9.7 MB down, on top of today's 11.1 MB; more if q must be about 2^64–2^77 to carry t ≥ 2^K headroom.
Extra GPU: one more GEMM at 7–10 digits, 1.4–2× an online GEMM.
Gateway CPU: same as PGW-LH (0.1 s per token).
Customer storage: the 28.5 GB hint plus a JIT buffer of 256–4096 tokens (1.8–28 GB).
One extra round trip per group, off the critical path.
options.security_model: Single provider, MLWE. No noise flooding is needed because W is public. Freivalds still checks the online product, and a pre-use Freivalds on W r (uW·r vs u·Wr) catches a bad preprocessing answer. Under that pre-use check, abort events are about discarded masks only.

summary:
The service learns W*x_hat anyway, so its share of the correlation can be zero, and two-party PCG machinery adds nothing beyond its LPN expansion step. Two options survive with single-provider security.

(B) z-store. The factory uploads z = W r - c to OUR provider, where c = PRG(seed) is a blind. The customer keeps only seeds. The service returns W x_hat - z = W x + c. The gateway subtracts c and runs an end-to-end Freivalds check on x. This also catches factory errors and closes threat T-29. Privacy reduces to PRG security, the same as today, under the same partner/provider non-collusion. Customer storage is about 0; ours is 6.95 MB/token.

(C) Dual-LPN-structured masks. r = [I|H'] e with e t-sparse and odd, uniform values mod 2^K. The gateway computes W r just in time from a one-time public table T = W H' (32.7 GB for 7B at N=2n). T can be computed by the provider and checked by the customer with Freivalds. Per-token storage is zero. Security is decisional dual-LPN over Z_2^K, with parameters set after the Liu-Wang-Yang-Yu EC'24 weight-halving attack: t about 300 at N=2n, about 150 at N=4n. Measured CPU gain over dense just-in-time W r is only 1.2-2x with a naive kernel (maybe 5-10x with an IFMA kernel, estimated). Its value is cutting gateway just-in-time compute, not storage, because dense just-in-time generation (about 0.31 s/token per 2 cores for 7B, extrapolated from measurement) already removes storage.

Two-party PCGs (VOLE/OLE/Ring-LPN/matrix triples) do not apply to a fixed matrix W held by the server, because W*(sparse) is dense. All subspace, sparse, reuse and rescaling masks are broken by explicit attacks.

options.name: C: dual-LPN structured masks with just-in-time W r from a one-time table
options.how_it_works: r = H e mod 2^K with H=[I_n|H'] public (H' uniform, stored once per input width) and e of weight t with a uniform random support and uniform odd values. W r = sum_{j<n} e_j W[:,j] + sum_{j>=n} e_j T[:,j-n], with T = W H' mod 2^K computed once. T is public data, so the provider can compute it, and the customer verifies it with Freivalds u^T T == (u^T W) H'. Cost per linear: m*t multiply-adds plus n*t*(N-n)/N for r. Implemented as a batched sparse-dense kernel, exact vs pgw ringmm.

Parameters: Prange exponent at weight t/2 >= 150 bits (accounts for the Liu-Wang-Yang-Yu EC'24 mod-2 weight halving and ~19 bits of DOOM multi-target over <=3e11 samples per H). summary:
Without new cryptography, three changes cut what the customer stores by about 50x or more. All numbers are for 1M Qwen2.5-7B tokens/day, K40A12, peak traffic at 3x the mean (estimate).

(1) Low-bit storage of W r (new, measured). The gateway only needs W8 r mod 2^b, where b_row = ceil(log2(2*qmax*sum|W8_row| + 1)). I measured the real per-row int8 weights of 3 of the 28 Qwen2.5-7B layers. That gives b = 29 bits for qkv, o and gate_up and 31 bits for down, against K = 40. Storage drops from 6.95 to 5.07 MB/token (-27%), or to 4.37 MB/token with A8. Decoding stays bit-exact (verified numerically). Freivalds still runs over the full 2^K ring, so integrity is unchanged in practice: errors at or above bit b do not change the decoded value. The factory also needs only r mod 2^b, which is 4 int8 limbs instead of 5 (-20% factory GEMM).

(2) Just-in-time CPU factory on AMX. I measured the pgw CLI and a prototype of my own on 7B layer shapes. The prototype generates r directly as uniform int8 digit planes, so no digit decomposition is needed. It made 6.5-7.6 7B tokens/s per core (measured on 2 of 4 cores, shared with other agents, so likely a lower bound). The stock pgw factory is 2-2.6x slower than this on the 0.5B pack. 1M tokens/day at 3x peak then needs about 4.3-5.3 cores, about $140-175/month on c7i vCPUs. A 15-minute buffer holds only 0.16-0.22 TB instead of 13.9 TB for a 2-day buffer. JIT generation also removes the 10-30% of masks burned by over-reservation.

(3) Prefix/KV caching on the gateway. This is not implemented yet; SPEC lists it as future work. Prompt tokens served from cache consume no masks. The gateway's KV cache costs 57 KB/token (fp16), about 120x less than the 6.95 MB of masks per token. Cited hit rates suggest it removes about 55% of masks for chat, 49% for RAG and 84% for agents (these savings are estimates). Combined with JIT and low-bit storage, an agent workload needs about 0.7 core and about 25 GB of buffer.

Storage tiering helps price but not volume. S3 Standard costs $23/TB-month against $80 for gp3, so the 13.9 TB baseline drops from $1,112 to $320/month. Required read bandwidth (80 MB/s mean, about 240 MB/s at peak) is within what S3 or HDD can deliver.

Model-side changes are mostly negative. GQA is already in place, and MQA would save only about 1.5%. A low-rank/SVD gate_up only removes masks if the gateway computes the A factor locally, and published quality is poor: SVD-LLM (ICLR 2025) reports LLaMA-7B WikiText-2 perplexity rising from 5.68 to 9.27 at 40% compression and 15.0 at 60%. MoE either leaks routing to us or needs masks for all experts. For Qwen3-30B-A3B that is 8.6 MB/token with routing leaked (more than 7B dense) and 112 MB/token without the leak.

Partial local compute is the best lever per local GFLOP. Computing qkv, o and gate_up on the gateway removes 92.8% of masks for 70.9% of the linear compute (0.70 MB saved per GOP), while down removes only 0.13 MB per GOP.

Critical caveat: JIT and local compute undermine the product case. Generating masks costs K/8 = 5 int8 GEMM limbs per token (65 GOP per 7B token). Computing the same linears locally in plaintext costs 1-2 limbs. On the same 2 cores, local int8 7B linears ran at 24-26 tok/s at batch 8 and 50-160 tok/s at batch 32 and above, against 13-15 tok/s for the JIT factory. A customer with enough CPU for a JIT factory could therefore run the 7B model locally 2.5-5x cheaper (about 1.4 cores at peak for 1M tokens/day, my estimate). Stored masks only make economic sense when they come from cheap, off-peak GPUs elsewhere (a T4 makes 169k tokens/hour, about $93/month for 1M tokens/day). Without a JIT factory, the realistic storage-reduction stack is low-bit storage plus prefix caching plus S3 tiering: 13.9 TB becomes about 1.6-5.2 TB at $130-410/month.

verdicts.option: B: RLWE token-batched GEMM preprocessing with fixed public a + one-time client hint (Q=2^64, t=2^40, N=4096)
verdicts.security_issues:
The core claim holds. The customer acts as its own dealer: it draws s, e and R, so there is no third party and no non-collusion assumption, and this is not the two-provider fallback in disguise. Privacy rests on RLWE with N=4096, logQ=64 and a ternary secret. The HE Standard's 128-bit limit for that N is logQ<=109 (cited, HomomorphicEncryption.org 2018). The other citations also check out: PRSD17 (STOC 2017) gives pseudorandomness for any modulus, and SimplePIR (USENIX Security 2023) reuses a fixed public matrix with a fresh secret and a client hint. The spec has three gaps that must be fixed before this counts as secure.
(1) The seed for a must come from the customer, or from a verifiable nothing-up-my-sleeve process. It must never come from us. If the server picks a, it can pick a=0 or a structured a, and then b=e+Delta*r reveals r directly. The prototype hardcodes aseed=99.
(2) The claim that leakage is at most 1 bit about a secret that is then discarded is wrong. The Freivalds vectors u and the stored uW are long-lived. Every accept or abort the server provokes in preprocessing tells it whether u.E==0 for an error E it chose, for example whether u_j is even when E=2^39 e_j. Repeated probing can strip u's entropy and then forge. Fix: draw fresh u per batch. Recomputing uW then costs about 6.5e9 MACs per vector per batch, which is about 1.6M per token and cheap. Also treat any preprocessing abort as an alert.
(3) Over Z_{2^40} the decrypted masks are uniform, so no range check can back up Freivalds in preprocessing. An error of 2-adic valuation 39 slips past each vector with probability 1/2. So c vectors give only 2^-c against high-valuation errors. Such errors are later caught deterministically, and independently of the data, by the online range check (|Wx - e_m| > bound). That makes the composite sound, but the spec must state c and this argument.
With (1)-(3), a malicious server can only cause aborts (DoS). Aborts in preprocessing do not depend on the data, so they reveal nothing about activations. The hint H=WA is a function of public data. The customer can compute it locally (about 28 min of CPU, derived from the measured 4.25 s per 4608x3584 slice) and does not need to trust us for it.
verdicts.numeric_issues:
I re-derived and confirmed: 831,488 inputs and 1,390,592 outputs per 7B token. Upload 6.65 MB (64 bits), download 7.65 MB (44 bits). Hint 1.39M x 4096 x 8 B = 45.6 GB. One-batch buffer 28.5 GB (= 4096 x 6.95 MB). Server 6.52e9 MAC/token, so 0.466 s at 0.0714 ns per MAC. Client 198 ns x 831k + 181 ns x 1.39M = 0.42 s. 70B hint 220 GB and buffer 138 GB.
Corrections:
(a) Per-token storage is 0 only at the margin. One decrypt yields one output feature for all 4096 tokens, so the first token of a batch is usable only after the whole batch has been decrypted. Decrypting a batch takes about 1,000 s on one core. Running just-in-time therefore needs double buffering: about 57 GB of buffer plus the 45.6 GB hint, so about 103 GB fixed (not 74 GB). That is still a drastic win at 1M tokens/day (today 7 TB/day) but a loss below about 15k tokens of buffered supply.
(b) The GPU rate rests on two team baselines that disagree by more than 3x. The given 169k/h for 7B at K40 conflicts with sizing.md's measured 550k slots/h for 8B at K48 on a T4. So the B rate is somewhere in 106k-440k tokens/h per T4. Both ends are derived; neither is measured at K=64. ring.py caps _MAX_K at 56, so K=64 also needs code changes and an exactness test.
(c) The extra bandwidth of 14.3 MB/token is about 1.3 Gbit/s sustained at 1M tokens/day, on top of about 1 Gbit/s online. Per batch that is 27 GB up and 31 GB down. If the gateway sits in a cloud, egress on the 6.65 TB/day upload is material: estimated at about $300-600/day at $0.05-0.09/GB list prices, not verified.
(d) Client CPU at 0.42 s/token means about 5 cores running 24/7 per 1M tokens/day (derived). The NTT client figure of 0.16 s is estimated, not measured.
(e) The noise margins were measured only on slices of about 5e6-6e7 coefficients. An analytic check (std of W e is at most 3.2 x 127 x sqrt(18944), about 2^15.8, against Delta/2 = 2^23) supports negligible failure over the 5.7e9 coefficients in a batch.
Practicality: realistic build time is 2-3 months, not 2-4 weeks. That covers a C++/HEXL NTT client mod 2^64, K=64 ringmm on GPU, a batch scheduler, the security write-up and an external crypto review. That fits inside 6 months.
verdicts.corrected_costs: Marginal storage 0 MB/token. Fixed footprint about 103 GB for 7B (45.6 GB hint + 2 x 28.5 GB batch buffers) or about 495 GB for 70B. Extra traffic 14.3 MB/token (about 1.3 Gbit/s at 1M tokens/day). Customer CPU 0.42 s/token measured in numpy (about 5 cores per 1M tokens/day). Our GPU: 106k-440k tokens/h per T4, derived.

verdicts.option: C: variant B plus upload compression (mask defined as high bits of u - a*s)
verdicts.security_issues:
As built (he_gemm64.py line 83: c = e - rem, rem = centered low 24 bits of u - a s), the upload leaks information about e. Here c = e - L with L uniform in [-2^23, 2^23). Whenever |c| exceeds 2^23, the value of c pins down the sign and a lower bound of e_ij. Combined with c mod 2^24 = (a s + e - u) mod 2^24, that gives a near-exact linear relation in s. The expected number of such coefficients is about E|e|/2^24 x 3.4e9, roughly 500 per batch (estimated), all under the same s. That shrinks the effective RLWE dimension and voids the claimed reduction. The argument that c reveals only a*s+e mod 2^24 is therefore false for this construction.
The fix is easy and gives an even smaller upload. Send c = centered((a s + e - u) mod 2^24), which is 24 bits. Define the mask as r = (u + c - a s - e)/2^24 mod 2^40. Then the server's view is exactly a function of an RLWE sample mod 2^24, and the high bits are pseudorandom by a clean hybrid argument. The 'a must be client-chosen' and Freivalds-reuse issues from B apply as well.
verdicts.numeric_issues: The 25-bit upload of 2.60 MB/token follows from 831,488 x 25 bits. The fixed variant needs 24 bits, which gives 2.49 MB/token and a total extra of about 10.1 MB/token. The client encrypt time was measured at 786 ns per element, unoptimised, i.e. 0.90 s/token. The 'close to B' figure after optimisation is an estimate.
verdicts.corrected_costs: Fixed variant: upload 2.49 MB + download 7.65 MB = 10.1 MB/token extra. Same 103 GB fixed footprint and server cost as B.

overall:
The track is mostly sound. Its arithmetic checks out and its core security model holds. Token-batched RLWE preprocessing (B, and A without the hint) is a genuine single-provider way to move the mask factory onto our GPU. Customer storage stops growing per token. What remains is a fixed footprint: about 103 GB for 7B in B once double buffering is counted (not 74 GB), or about 57 GB in A. No trusted dealer or non-collusion assumption is hidden in it, because the customer generates its own secrets.

Must-fix gaps:
(1) The seed for a must be chosen by the customer or be verifiably random. If we chose it, a=0 would expose r.
(2) The 'leaks at most 1 bit about a discarded secret' claim is wrong. The Freivalds vectors are long-lived and can be probed through aborts. Use fresh u per batch, which is cheap.
(3) A preprocessing Freivalds check mod 2^40 has no range check behind it. The spec needs a stated vector count c, plus the argument that the online range check catches high-valuation mask errors.
(4) Variant C as implemented leaks noise information through the representative of c. The fix sends the centered (a s + e - u) mod 2^24 (24 bits) and defines r from that.

On the numbers, the cost moves from storage to bandwidth (+10-14 MB/token, about 1-1.3 Gbit/s at 1M tokens/day) and to customer CPU (about 5 cores per 1M tokens/day in numpy). The GPU rate cannot be pinned down because the team's two factory baselines disagree by more than 3x: 106k-440k tokens/h per T4. ringmm also needs K=64 support.

On practicality, about 2-3 months including a C++ NTT client and an external crypto review is feasible within 6 months. Recommend fixed-C (24-bit upload) on top of B, with fixes (1)-(3). Use A if the 45.6 GB hint is unacceptable.

verdicts.option: PGW-LH: hinted MLWE masking (Delphi preprocessing folded into the online call)
verdicts.security_issues:
I could not refute the core claim. The service sees A and H = W·A (both independent of customer data) and v = Δx − (<a,s>+e) mod q. By decision-MLWE with a fresh secret per (group, layer, linear) under one public A, v is pseudorandom. Many secrets under one A is the standard hybrid argument. Partial release of a group's coefficients is fine because any subset of pseudorandom values is pseudorandom.

Decoding is algebraically correct: z + C = ΔWx − We, and C = <WA, s> = W<a,s>. No factory, no partner and no non-collusion assumption are hidden in it. It is genuinely single-provider, so it is not the two-provider fallback in disguise.

Integrity, full-z mode: Freivalds over F_q fails with probability 1 − 1/q for any z ≠ W·v. Whether it aborts depends only on (u, δ), so selective failure leaks nothing. There is no online preprocessing phase the provider could corrupt. The only provider-supplied preprocessing object is H, and it is checked at setup with u^T H = (u^T W) A.

Caveats and corrections:
(a) Truncated-z mode: the claim that 'an abort leaks at most 1 bit' is wrong. Freivalds runs on the decoded y, so a rounding flip depends on the secret We. The non-abort event is informative as well: the service can add deviations near Δ/2 that are absorbed or not depending on We. The real bound is about log2(number of checks until the first abort) bits, and only if the gateway aborts permanently with no restart under live seeds. Leaking e is dangerous: if e were learned, the scheme degrades to LWE whose error is Δx, i.e. data-dependent, after modulus switching to t. Ship full-z only and drop truncated-z.
(b) The seed for A must be chosen by the gateway and never by the service. A trapdoored A would break privacy. The design already does this; it must be a hard spec rule.
(c) Single-use slots are critical. Reusing a (group seed, coefficient) slot gives v1 − v2 = Δ(x1 − x2) exactly, with no noise. Retry and resend logic must never resend with the same slot.
(d) Small error in design.md: each secret gets n_in ring samples (3,584 or 18,944), not '≈30k'. Security is unaffected.
(e) Security level, my estimate: a primal-uSVP core-SVP calculation (my script usvp.py, 2016 estimate) gives block size β ≈ 445 (0.292β ≈ 130) at n = 2560, log q = 56, σ_e = 3.24, σ_s = 1. For comparison the HE-Standard 128-bit point (n = 2048, log q = 54) gives β ≈ 340 under the same model. So the parameters are comfortably at or above HE-Standard 128-bit. I verified the HE-Standard figures 54 and 109 from memory only. A formal lattice-estimator run is still required before shipping.
verdicts.numeric_issues:
I re-derived the following from first principles; all match the track:
- Rows of output features: Σm·L = 49,664 × 28 = 1.39M.
- Rows of input features: Σn·L = (3,584·3 + 18,944) × 28 = 831k. Total 2.22M rows.
- Hint: 1.39M × 2,560 coefficients × 8 B = 28.5 GB. Packed at 7 B it is 24.9 GB.
- A: (3,584 + 18,944) × 2,560 × 7 B ≈ 0.40 GB.
- Group buffer: 2.22M × 256 × 8 B = 4.55 GB (4.0 GB packed).
- Up: 831k × 7 B = 5.82 MB. Down: 1.39M × 7 B = 9.73 MB. Truncated down at 36 bits: 6.26 MB.
- Gateway CPU: 2.22M × 46.3 ns = 0.103 core-s per token. The 46.3 ns is measured and plausible: 2,560 modmuls plus a 256-point INTT is about 11.9 µs per row.
- 70B: 6.72M output rows → hint 137.6 GB, down 47.0 MB. 4.26M input rows → up 29.8 MB. Buffer 22.5 GB. Today's 70B storage: 33.6 MB per token.
- GPU: 2 extra digit GEMMs ≈ 2.6e16 ops per 1M tokens. At 1,979 dense INT8 TOPS (H100 SXM, cited, correct) and 10–30% utilisation that is 44–131 s. Correct.
- Factory: 1e6 / 169k = 5.9 T4-hours per 1M tokens. Correct.
- Noise: the analytic σ(We) at n = 18,944 with all-127 weights is 127 × 3.24 × 137.6 ≈ 2^15.8. Measured 2^17.6 ≈ 3.5σ, which is consistent. The 2^21 budget is about 37σ, so the decoding failure probability is negligible.
- 7 balanced int8 digits suffice for residues mod q < 2^56 if the representative window [−0.502, 0.498]·2^56 is used. int32 accumulation is safe: 127·128·18,944 < 2^31.

Citations checked:
- SimplePIR (USENIX Security 2023): 121 MB hint per 1 GB database and about 10 GB/s per core. Confirmed (one version says 12.4 GB/s).
- BumbleBee (NDSS 2025): about 8 min per token for LLaMA-7B; ePrint 2023/1678 says about 14 min. Confirmed.
- Not checked: NEXUS/BOLT, Rhombus and Cheetah figures. They are not load-bearing.

Missing number: the 1.4× GPU cost is analytic only and has not been benchmarked.

Practicality issues not quantified by the track:
(1) Prefill bursts. Pads are produced at about 10 tokens/s per scalar core. A 32k-token prompt with an empty buffer needs about 3,300 core-s, roughly 100 s on 32 cores. Buffering 32k tokens in advance costs about 590 GB. The gateway CPU, or AVX-512 IFMA (3–8× estimated, not measured), becomes the prefill throughput cap.
(2) For 70B the 138 GB hint must be streamed once per 256-token group. From NVMe at about 3 GB/s that is roughly 46 s per group, which caps throughput near 5.6 tokens/s unless the hint sits in RAM or N' = 1024 is used.
(3) The 3–5 engineer-week estimate is optimistic for production. It covers an NTT/IFMA gateway, a mod-q digit kernel, wire and spec migration and a lattice audit, and an external cryptographic review is advisable. A realistic plan is a prototype in about 1 month and production in about 2–3 months, which fits the 6-month window.

verdicts.option: Variant A: JIT HE preprocessing, Delphi-shaped, online protocol unchanged
verdicts.security_issues:
The base form holds: the gateway encrypts r under MLWE, decodes Wr, and runs a pre-use Freivalds check u·(Wr) = (uW)·r. That check costs O(n + m) and catches a bad preprocessing answer before any use, so abort events involve discarded masks only.

The claimed alternative, Delphi's 'service keeps s/S' form, does NOT move the buffer to our side. The gateway still has to hold its share Wr − S, which is n_out elements per token, the same size as today's mask. In addition, Freivalds then needs u·S per token. That scalar can be derived as (uW)·r − u·(Wr − S), but this is not described.

The decoding of Wr mod 2^K needs q ≡ 1 mod 2^K, or q ≳ 2^62–2^84, because |Wr| reaches about 2^61 over the integers. The track's '2^64–2^77' range is roughly right.
verdicts.numeric_issues:
Extra network is about +5.8 MB up and +9.7 MB down per token at q ≈ 2^56. It is more at q ≈ 2^64+: about 6.6 MB up and 11.1 MB down at 8 bytes.

The extra GEMM needs 8–11 digits rather than 7–10 if q is 2^64–2^84.

The JIT buffer is 6.95 MB per token × 256–4,096 tokens = 1.8–28.5 GB. Correct.

The Delphi/Gazelle ResNet-32 figure (158 s, 8 GB) was not verified and is not load-bearing.

overall:
PGW-LH survives the adversarial review on security and arithmetic.

- Privacy rests on decision-MLWE with a single provider. There is no hidden trusted dealer and no non-collusion party, so it is not the two-provider fallback in disguise.
- Full-z Freivalds over F_q gives sound integrity with abort events that do not depend on the data. The provider's only preprocessing input, H, is checked at setup.
- All storage, network and CPU numbers re-derive correctly, apart from 8-byte versus 7-byte packing. Customer storage per token goes from 6.95 MB to 0, with a fixed hint of about 28.5 GB plus a 4.6 GB buffer.
- A crude primal-uSVP estimate puts (n = 2560, log q = 56) above the HE-Standard 128-bit point. A formal lattice-estimator run is still owed.

Required corrections:
1. Drop truncated-z mode. Its '1 bit at abort' leakage claim is false: non-abort events leak information about the noise e too, and the bound is about log2(#checks), and only with a permanent abort.
2. Variant A's 'service keeps S' form does not move storage to our side.
3. Hard spec rules are needed: the gateway alone chooses the seed for A, and no slot is ever reused, including on retries.

Practical risks the track under-states:
- The gateway CPU caps prefill bursts at about 10 tokens/s per scalar core.
- For 70B, streaming the 138 GB hint from NVMe caps throughput at about 6 tokens/s unless the hint is in RAM or N' = 1024 is used.
- The 1.4× GPU overhead is unmeasured.
- 3–5 engineer-weeks is optimistic. Production plus a crypto review looks like about 2–3 months, which still fits the 6-month window.

Recommendation: adopt PGW-LH in full-z mode as the primary path. Sources: SimplePIR (USENIX Security 2023, https://www.usenix.net/system/files/usenixsecurity23-henzinger.pdf) and BumbleBee (NDSS 2025, https://ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/bumblebee-secure-two-party-inference-framework-for-large-transformers ; ePrint 2023/1678). verdicts.security_issues: The core argument is right. The provider sees (x_hat = x + r, z = W r - c), and with c and r pseudorandom and unknown to it, both are jointly uniform. Without c the provider would get W x, so the blind is essential. This adds no new non-collusion assumption beyond the baseline: the factory (partner) knows r and c, so partner+provider collusion breaks privacy, exactly as today. Be honest that whenever the factory is a partner rather than the customer, the base PGW design is already a two-party non-collusion model (an offline dealer plus one server). B is not the circular second compute provider, but it is a trusted-dealer assumption. B makes collusion easier and less auditable, because the partner now has a direct high-volume channel into our infrastructure (slot IDs, timing and volume metadata too). Recommendation: the customer, not the partner, pushes or authorizes uploads, and B is used with a customer-run factory where possible. Integrity: the end-to-end Freivalds check u.y == (uW).x is algebraically identical to today's check, so it also catches factory errors (closes T-29). Correction to notes.md line 22: the claim 'an abort depends only on (error, u), never on x' is false once the range check is included. A deviation with high 2-adic valuation that slips past Freivalds with probability about 2^-(h*c) makes the range-check outcome depend on y = W x + delta. This selective-failure leak is pre-existing, bounded by pgw.core.freivalds.soundness_bits, and not worsened by B, but it must be stated correctly. Slot-swapping or replaying z gives deviations independent of x, so they are caught. Each c and slot must be single-use and enforced by the gateway, not the provider.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Customer storage of about 0 is correct apart from the seeds and a small just-in-time buffer. Provider storage of 6.95 MB/token is correct, but only as a rolling buffer: 1 hour at 1M tokens/day is about 290 GB (estimated). The track omits that B does NOT reduce factory compute (T4 about 169k tokens/h measured, so about 6 T4-hours/day per 1M tokens) and does not reduce transfer volume. 7 TB/day equals about 650 Mbit/s sustained (derived), or about 2.6 Gbit/s burst at full T4 output (1.17 TB/h). If the factory is a cloud GPU sending over the internet, egress at roughly $0.05-0.09/GB (AWS EC2 internet data-transfer-out tiers, cited from memory, not re-verified) costs about $350-630/day per 1M 7B tokens. That is about 100x the GPU cost (about $2-3/day estimated), so bandwidth, not storage, becomes the dominant cost. Same-region or private-link transfer between the customer's factory account and our provider region cuts this to about $0-0.01/GB (estimated), but the factory must stay in an account we do not control. Factory: unchanged GPU work (about 6 T4-h/day per 1M tokens). Transfer: 7 TB/day per 1M tokens, about $350-630/day if over internet egress, about $0-70/day if same-region.

verdicts.option: C: dual-LPN structured masks with just-in-time W r from a one-time table
verdicts.security_issues: (1) The assumption is plausible but unverified. Decisional dual-LPN over Z_2^K with a uniform public H and fresh noise per (token, linear) is a standard-style assumption, and the cited Liu-Wang-Yang-Yu EUROCRYPT 2024 paper is verified (LNCS 14656, artifacts.iacr.org/eurocrypt/2024/a1; abstract confirms the noise-weight halving and the 'up to 40 bits' overestimate). The parameters, however, rest only on a Prange closed form. I reproduced Prange at about 150-152 bits for (N=2n, w=150) and (N=4n, w=75) for n=3584 and 18944 (measured with my script). The official estimator was never run, and the code dimension (3584-28672) is far smaller than the usual PCG regime. Until then the security is unsupported and should be treated as such. There is also an internal inconsistency: with odd noise values the mod-2 reduction keeps the full weight t, so t = 2w is a conservative double count, not the cited attack. (2) A new selective-failure channel exists. If the provider computes T = W H', any error in T produces a W r error that depends on the secret support of e, so aborts leak mask-support bits. The single-vector Freivalds check u^T T == (u^T W) H' has low soundness for high-valuation errors over Z_2^K. Fix: the gateway builds T itself (about 3584 dense-token-equivalents, about 20 min on 2 cores for N=2n, estimated), or it verifies T with full multi-vector soundness and hard-halts on any later abort.
verdicts.numeric_issues: The storage and operation counts re-derive correctly: T is 32.6 GB at N=2n (= 6.525e9 MAC x 5 B) and 98 GB at N=4n; H' is 1.86 GB but could be regenerated from a public seed (about 0 GB); 5.4e8 and 3.0e8 ops/token are correct. The track omits that batch-4096 table streaming needs a buffer of finished W r: 4096 x 6.95 MB = about 28 GB. The decisive refutation is practical. I measured plaintext linear layers on this loaded machine at 2 threads: f64 GEMM 26 ps/MAC, i.e. 0.17 s/token for all 7B linears; f32 GEMM 9 ps/MAC, i.e. 0.06 s/token (not exact for the down layer); int8 VNNI would be faster still (estimated). So C's 0.15-0.27 s/token, and the 'dense just-in-time W r 0.31 s/token' baseline, cost MORE gateway CPU than running the linears locally in plaintext. A gateway that can afford C does not need the outsourced service at all. Even the speculative 5-10x IFMA kernel (estimated, not built) only reaches parity with local int8 inference. The track's own statement that dense just-in-time generation 'already removes storage' is wrong for the same reason.
verdicts.corrected_costs: One-time: 32.6-98 GB table plus about 28 GB of W r buffer if batched at 4096. Per token: about 0.15-0.27 s per 2 cores, versus about 0.06-0.17 s per 2 cores for local plaintext linears (measured). This defeats the purpose of outsourcing.

overall: B survives. It is the actionable result: customer mask storage drops to about 0 by having the factory upload a c-blinded z = W r - c to our provider, with no new trust assumption beyond the baseline factory/provider non-collusion. Two things must be said plainly. First, a partner-run factory already makes PGW a dealer-plus-server non-collusion model, so prefer a customer-run factory. Second, B moves the 7 TB/day per 1M 7B tokens problem from customer disk to transfer (about 650 Mbit/s sustained). That transfer can cost $350-630/day over internet egress (cited from memory, unverified) unless the factory is co-located in the same region. B also does not reduce factory compute. Its build effort is small and fits a 6-month startup timeline. Also fix the notes' claim that aborts never depend on x: the range check makes them depend on x, which is pre-existing and bounded by soundness_bits. C fails. Its LPN parameters are checked only with Prange (I reproduced about 150 bits; the official Liu et al. EC'24 estimator was not run). It opens a selective-failure leak of the mask support if T comes from the provider. Most decisively, its per-token gateway CPU (0.15-0.27 s per 2 cores) exceeds the cost of computing the 7B linears locally in plaintext (0.06-0.17 s per 2 cores, measured here), so it, and dense just-in-time W r, undermine the reason for outsourcing. verdicts.option: Low-bit storage of W r (truncate to the decode bound)
verdicts.security_issues: Privacy is unchanged: x_hat is the same and r is still uniform mod 2^K, regenerated from the seed. Generating r as signed int8 digit planes is a bijection onto Z_{2^40}, so r stays uniform. Integrity against the service holds, but the guarantee changes from 'service response correct mod 2^K' to 'decoded output correct'. Errors with 2-adic valuation v >= b do not change the mod-2^b decode. Errors with v < b pass Freivalds with probability at most 2^-(K-v) <= 2^-(K-b+1). The whitepaper's Theorem 3 and pgw soundness_bits (h = K - ceil(log2(4*qmax*127*n))) assume a full-K decode followed by the generic range check, so they must be re-derived as h = K - b + 1. That is usually better: down at A12 gives about 10 bits against about 5 today with the generic bound. One real loss: SPEC 3.2 relies on the gateway range check to catch gross factory errors in W r. With full-K storage, a garbage W r lands in range with probability about 2^-9. With a tight b-bit store it lands in range with probability about 0.5 or more, so factory faults go undetected unless the factory self-check or the planned T-29 spot-check is mandatory. A per-row b is also a function of the public W, so it leaks nothing.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Re-derived: per layer (46,080 x 29 + 3,584 x 31) bits = 180,928 B; x 28 = 5.066 MB/token (correct). Baseline 49,664 x 5 x 28 = 6.953 MB (correct). Worst-case bound check: qkv/o/gate_up with n = 3584 have a generic bound of 31 bits and measured 29; down with n = 18944 has a generic bound of 34 bits and measured 31. Plausible, but b is the maximum over 3 of 28 layers of the author's own absmax quantization, not the pgw pack. A single outlier row in another layer adds a bit to that linear under per-linear packing. Expect about 5.1-5.3 MB/token until all 28 layers are measured; per-row packing is robust to this. The '-20% factory GEMM' (4 limbs instead of 5) is correct, because 32 bits >= 31.
verdicts.corrected_costs: No extra cost. Storage drops 25-27%. Factory GEMM drops 20%.

verdicts.option: JIT CPU mask factory on the gateway's AMX cores
verdicts.security_issues: Security is fine: the customer runs the factory, as today, and the PRG assumption is unchanged.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Re-derived: 6.52 G MAC/token x 5 limbs x 2 = 65.2 GOP (correct). 13-15 tok/s on 2 threads gives 0.85-0.99 TOPS (consistent). 11.57 tok/s mean / 7 tok/s per core = 1.65 cores, 5 at 3x peak; $0.0446 x 5.34 x 730 = $174 (correct). Caveats: (a) The measurement was on 2 'cores' of a shared VM, which are probably vCPUs. AMX is one unit per physical core, so the per-vCPU price may overstate the throughput per dollar if 2 vCPUs share an AMX tile unit. (b) The track's own caveat is decisive. The factory does at least K/8 = 4-5 limbs of the same GEMM shapes that plaintext local inference does in 1-2 limbs. Any customer able to run a JIT factory can run the 7B linears locally for 2.5-5x less compute (measured 24-26 tok/s at batch 8, and 50-160 tok/s batched, on the same 2 threads). The option therefore defeats the product premise (no customer-site compute for linears). It is only rational if latency or batch-1 memory bandwidth makes local inference infeasible, which the 7B measurements do not show. Treat it as a buffer-shrinking tactic for partner-run or off-peak GPUs, not a customer-gateway design.
verdicts.corrected_costs: $140-175/month CPU for 1M tok/day at 3x peak (if vCPU = AMX-capable core; up to 2x more if AMX is per physical core). Buffer 0.16-0.22 TB. Dominated by local plaintext inference at about 1.4 cores (estimate).

verdicts.security_issues: No cryptographic change. A new metadata leak exists: the service sees row counts per call, which today reveal the total prompt length. With caching it sees only the uncached suffix length. Combined with timing, this lets it infer that a request continues an earlier conversation or reuses a known document or system prompt, and how long the shared prefix is. That is linkability and access-pattern leakage beyond today's. It can be mitigated by padding call sizes or batching, which costs masks. The plaintext KV is kept at rest on the customer's gateway, so this is a customer-side data-retention issue only.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Verified: SGLang (arXiv 2312.07104, NeurIPS 2024) says 'cache hit rate ranges from 50% to 99%' and reports 52.4% (LLaVA-Next-34B) and 74.1% (Vicuna-33B) in production. SVD-LLM values were not part of this option. KV size 28 x 2 x 4 x 128 x 2 B = 57,344 B (correct). The savings estimates are optimistic. The chat figure uses the higher of the two Arena hit rates (74.1%; 52.4% gives about 39% saved). Those rates come from a large multi-tenant service, while one customer's gateway with bounded RAM will see fewer cross-user hits. Retaining multi-turn KV across sessions also needs real RAM or disk: a 100k-token working set is 5.7 GB. Blended per-token masks with low-bit storage: chat 2.3-3.1 MB, RAG about 2.6 MB, agent about 0.8 MB (estimated). Hit rates must be measured on the customer's own logs.
verdicts.corrected_costs: Gateway KV RAM/disk of a few GB to tens of GB; engineering effort is medium.

verdicts.option: Partial local compute of linear groups on the gateway
verdicts.security_issues: Local compute leaks nothing, so security holds trivially.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Re-derived: mask shares 9.3/7.2/76.3/7.2% and MAC shares 7.1/5.5/58.3/29.1% (correct). 5 B per 7,168 ops gives 0.70 MB/GOP at 1 limb (correct). Down-only storage is 3584 x 28 x 31 bits = 0.39 MB/token low-bit, or 0.50 MB at full K. This is not a storage optimization. Doing 71% of the linear MACs locally means the customer needs inference-class CPU. The provider would keep only the down projection (29% of compute), which contradicts the 'no customer-site hardware' premise and makes the product nearly pointless for 7B. Batch-1 local decode is memory-bound: 7.6 GB of weights at about 21 GB/s gives about 3 tok/s on 2 cores (measured 3.2), so latency on a small gateway is poor.
verdicts.corrected_costs: Gateway with roughly 16 cores and more than 100 GB/s of memory bandwidth for interactive 7B latency (estimate).

verdicts.security_issues: Security is unchanged: segments are AES-GCM encrypted with destroyable DEKs. Putting segments in a cloud bucket adds a cloud provider as a holder of ciphertext. That is not a privacy break, but the customer's data-residency policy must allow it.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Re-derived: 13.9 TB x $80 = $1,112 and x $23 = $320/month; 6.95 TB / 64 MB = 108.6k PUTs, about $0.54/day (correct). Missing cost: if the gateway is not in the same AWS region as the bucket (on-prem, other cloud, or another region), every byte of masks is read out of S3. At about 7 TB/day that is 210 TB/month. At AWS internet egress of about $0.05-0.09/GB (AWS data-transfer pricing, tiered; cited from memory, verify), that is about $11k-19k/month, which dwarfs the savings. Also, ingress from an off-site factory needs a sustained 80 MB/s (0.64 Gbit/s) upload. The option holds only for gateways co-located in-region.
verdicts.corrected_costs: $320/month for S3 Standard storage in-region. Add $11k-19k/month egress if the gateway sits outside the bucket's region (estimate).

verdicts.security_issues: MoE with active-only masks leaks routing, which is unacceptable, as the track itself says. Low-rank gate_up removes masks only by moving compute local, which has the same problem as partial local compute.
verdicts.numeric_issues: Verified: SVD-LLM (arXiv 2403.07378, ICLR 2025) Table 1 gives LLaMA-7B WikiText-2 perplexity 5.68 / 7.73 / 9.27 / 15.00 / 31.79. Re-derived: MQA gives 4608 to 3840 rows, saving 0.107 MB (1.5%). Qwen3-30B-A3B: (5120 + 2048 + 8 x 3584) x 48 x 5 B = 8.6 MB; all 128 experts gives 111.8 MB (correct). Quality loss, retraining effort and the security problems make this a non-option.
verdicts.corrected_costs: Retraining plus a quality-evaluation harness; not viable within 6 months.

verdicts.option: Combination: JIT CPU factory + low-bit + prefix caching (+K32A8)
verdicts.security_issues: This inherits the new prefix-cache metadata leak and the weaker factory-error detection from low-bit storage. Otherwise it is single-provider with the PRG assumption.
verdicts.numeric_issues: The headline field says 5.07 MB/token, which ignores the prefix savings (blended about 0.8-2.8). The JIT part is dominated by local inference (about 1.4 cores for all linears, against 0.7-2.2 cores of factory for the same load). That is the track's own figure, and it makes the combination self-defeating as a customer-gateway design. Also, at K32A8 pgw requires h >= 20 bits, and SPEC says very wide K32A8 layers cannot reach that floor. With low-bit decode h = 32 - b + 1, and b is about 25-27 at A8, giving 6-8 bits per vector, so 3-4 check vectors are needed. That is workable, but must be stated. The realistic stack is low-bit + prefix caching + in-region tiering, with masks from an off-peak partner or T4 GPU.
verdicts.corrected_costs: Without JIT, at 1M tok/day with a 2-day buffer: about 1.6 TB (agent) to 5.2 TB (RAG); $37-120/month on S3 in-region or $130-410/month on gp3, plus about $93/month of T4 time scaled by the uncached fraction (estimate).

overall:
Most of the track's numbers check out. I re-derived the 7B mask sizes (6.95 MB/token at full K, 5.07 MB/token low-bit), the 65 GOP/token factory cost, the cost model, the KV size and the MoE counts. The SVD-LLM and SGLang citations were confirmed against the arXiv texts; I did not verify the others.

Low-bit storage is the solid, cheap win, about 27% less storage. Two caveats:
- The soundness proof (whitepaper Theorem 3 and soundness_bits) has to be rewritten for mod-2^b decoding.
- Truncating removes the gateway range check's detection of gross factory errors in W r. A factory self-check or spot-check becomes mandatory.

Prefix caching is the biggest volume lever, roughly 40-85% fewer masks. But the savings are estimated from large multi-tenant traces, and the provider gains a new metadata leak: by seeing uncached suffix lengths it can link requests that reuse a conversation or document prefix.

Two options fail on product grounds, not on security:
- The JIT CPU factory needs more compute than running the same linears locally, by the track's own measurement.
- Partial local compute leaves the provider almost nothing to do.

S3 tiering only holds if the gateway is in the bucket's region. Otherwise about 7 TB/day of reads costs roughly $11-19k/month in egress.

Nothing here is a cryptographic breakthrough, and none of it hides a second-party or trusted-dealer assumption. The realistic 6-month stack is low-bit storage + prefix caching + in-region tiering, with masks made off-peak by a partner or T4 GPU. That gives about 0.8-2.8 MB per 7B token, against 6.95 MB today.
